label: JZ Mock D · Paper 1 · Question 15
source: JZ Mock D · Paper 1 · Question 15 · Publisher worked solution
knowledgePattern: Locate an incircle centre using perpendicular radii, then test squared distances

hints.title: Find the centre before testing points
hints.body: Sketch the three sides of the triangle. The centre of an inscribed circle lies on the lines that halve the triangle’s angles.
hints.recap: The circle’s centre is equally far from the sides it touches.
hints.pitfall: Use the angle bisectors inside the triangle.
hints.pause: Mark the angle at the origin and the angle where the sloping line meets the x-axis.

recall.reminder: A radius to a tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent line.

hints.title: Use the angle at the origin
hints.body: The line y=3x makes an angle of 60∘ with the positive x-axis. The centre lies halfway inside this angle.
hints.recap: A line through the origin making angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> with the x-axis has equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>.
hints.pitfall: The centre’s height will also be the radius, because the circle touches <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
hints.pause: Write the equation of this first angle bisector.

recall.reminder: A line through the origin making angle <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> with the x-axis has equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math>.

hints.title: Use the other angle bisector
hints.body: Find where x+y=1+2+3 meets the x-axis. Its slope is −1, so the interior angle there is 45∘. Use the given value of tan22.5∘ to draw the line halfway inside that angle.
hints.recap: Two angle bisectors meet at the circle’s centre.
hints.pitfall: At this vertex, measure horizontally towards the left, into the triangle.
hints.pause: Write the second line, solve where the two bisectors meet, and find the radius.

recall.reminder: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> gives the opposite side divided by the adjacent side in a right-angled triangle.

hints.title: Compare each point with the circle
hints.body: For a centre (h,k) and radius r, a point is inside when (x−h)2+(y−k)2<r2.
hints.recap: Squared distance avoids an unnecessary square root.
hints.pitfall: Equality means the point is on the circle, not inside it.
hints.pause: Test the options. A horizontal or vertical distance already larger than the radius is enough to rule a point out.

recall.reminder: Squared distance avoids an unnecessary square root.

solution:
1. Find two lines through the centre. The centre lies on the internal angle bisectors. The angle at the origin is 60∘, so its bisector is y=xtan30∘=x/3.

Write L=1+2+3. The side x+y=L meets the x-axis at (L,0) and makes an interior angle of 45∘ there. Its internal bisector is y=(2−1)(L−x).

2. Find the centre and radius. The two bisectors meet where x/3=(2−1)(1+2+3−x). Substituting x=3 makes both sides 1, since (2−1)(2+1)=1. These two nonparallel lines have one intersection, so the centre is (3,1). The circle touches y=0, hence its radius is 1.

3. Check the points. For A the horizontal distance is 3−1/2>1. For B the vertical distance is already 1 and the horizontal distance is nonzero. For C the vertical distance is 3/2>1. For E the horizontal distance is 3−3>1. These points are outside.

For D, the squared distance is (1−3)2+(5/3−1)2=40/9−23. This is less than 1 because it is equivalent to 31<183, and squaring these positive quantities gives 961<972. Thus D lies inside. Answer D.
